notes.text: The purposes of God's love concerning Sarah, ver. 9-15.

The purposes of God's wrath concerning Sodom. (1.) The discovery God made to Abraham of his design to destroy Sodom, ver. 16-22. (2.) The intercession Abraham made for Sodom, ver. 23-33.

1. This appearance of God to Abraham seems to have had in it more of freedom and familiarity, and less of grandeur and majesty, than those we have hitherto read of, and therefore more resembles that great visit which in the fulness of time the Son of God was to make to the world. He sat in the tent-door in the heat of the day - Not so much to repose himself, as to seek an opportunity of doing good, by giving entertainment to strangers.

2. And lo three men - These three men were three spiritual heavenly beings, now assuming human shapes, that they might be visible to Abraham, and conversable with him. Some think they were all three created angels; others, that one of them was the Son of God. He bowed himself towards the ground - Religion doth not destroy but improve good manners, and teaches us to honour all men.

Where is Sarah thy wife? — By naming her, they gave intimation to Abraham, that tho' they seemed strangers, yet they well knew him and his family: by enquiring after her, they shewed a kind concern for the family of one, whom they found respectful to them. And by speaking of her, she over-hearing it, they drew her to listen to what was farther to be said.
I will certainly return unto thee — And visit thee. God will return to those that bid him welcome.

Sarah laughed within herself — It was not a laughter of faith, like Abraham's, chap. xvii, 17, but a laughter of doubting and distrust. The great objection which Sarah could not get over was her age. I am waxed old, and past child-bearing in a course of nature, especially having been hitherto barren, and which magnifies the difficulty, My Lord is old also. Observe here, That Sarah calls Abraham her Lord, and the Holy Ghost takes notice of it to her honour, and recommends it to the imitation of all Christian wives, 1Pe iii, 6. Sarah obeyed Abraham calling him Lord, in token of respect and subjection.

glossa.text: « And the Lord appeared to him in the vale of Mambre. » ((ISID. in Gen. )) Abraham bears a threefold figure: the first, of the Saviour, who leaving his kindred came into the world; the second, of the Father, because he offered up his only Son; the third (which appears in this place), of the saints who received the coming of Christ with joy . The tabernacle of Abraham signifies Jerusalem, where in their season the prophets and the apostles dwelt, and Christ at his coming was received by them that believed, and by them that believed not was hanged upon the tree.

« Three men. » Three men announce the coming of Christ, whom two angels accompany, Moses according to some, and Elias; the one a lawgiver, who in the law showed the coming of the Lord: the other, who is to come at the end, to announce the second coming of Christ and to preach his Gospel. Whence, when the Lord was transfigured on the mountain, they are seen with him. « He saw three, and adored one, » showing namely the Saviour, whose coming he was awaiting. Whence: « Abraham saw my day and was glad ((Joan. VIII)). » For he foresaw the mystery of the sacrament to come. Whence he washed their feet, that he might show the purification of the laver that was to be at the end of the world; for the feet signify the last things.

« Whom when he had seen. » *((GREG., lib. IX Moral., c. 51.)) Morally.* Abraham ran to meet three angels, because the man and master of the house, that is, the spiritual understanding, ought in the knowledge of the Trinity to pass beyond the barriers of the flesh, and as it were to go out at the door of the lowest dwelling. Let the care of the flesh, which Sara signifies, not appear abroad for ostentation, but behind the man's back, that is, under the discretion of the spirit, intent upon necessary things alone, let it not know how to uncover itself shamelessly, but to govern itself modestly.

((Ibid., lib. XXVIII, c. 4)). Abraham could not have seen the angels, received them into his lodging and set food before them, unless they had taken a body out of air: for they would not appear, they would not take food, unless they had a solid body of a heavenly element. Nor is it strange that now they are called angels, now the Lord, because they are called angels who minister without, and the Lord is shown, who commands them within.

« But I will fetch. » He returns to the offices of hospitality, which can be shown even to angels, when they take a bodily form out of the elements: which Abraham understanding, adored the Godhead in unity, and ministered to the angelic dispensation in visible form.

« Three sata. » These things are said in the type of the Church, which out of the three parts of the world is gathered into the unity of faith, and as bread without leaven is baked by the fire of the Holy Ghost.

((STRAB.)) A satum is a kind of measure. Three sata signify the three sons of Noah, out of whom the whole race of men was sown abroad. Therefore the Church is signified, or the evangelical doctrine that is to be sown throughout the whole world, and to be multiplied in the three parts of the world, Asia, Africa and Europe.

« Three sata, » of which Sara makes the loaves baked under the ashes, signify the three sons of Noah, out of whom the whole race of men was born: who, believing in the divine Trinity, were sprinkled with the water of baptism through Sara, that is, the Church, and were brought together into the one bread of the body of Christ. These are the three sata of meal which the woman in the Gospel leavened: they are unleavened loaves, because without the leaven of malice, and the anguish [ *Al.,* rancore] of wickedness, and the fervour of perverse doctrine, the unity of believers ought to be.

« Baked under the ashes. » They are baked under the ashes, that being baked by the vapour of the Holy Ghost through repentance for their sins, they may be made food acceptable to God.

« A calf most tender. » The tender and fatted calf is the body of Christ, which for the salvation of the world was offered up upon the tree of the cross. This is the calf that is killed for the prodigal son.

« Butter and milk » he set before them with the flesh of the calf, because milk signifies the old law; whence I Cor. III: « Milk I gave you to drink, not meat, » etc. For he had delivered to them the commandment of the law, as milk pressed out of the breasts of the two tables, that is the testament of faith, because they could not yet take the solid meat of the evangelical doctrine. The most rich and fat butter is the evangelical testimony, which like oil is given to the faithful for a sign. He set the calf before them with milk and butter, because neither can the body of the Lord be without the milk of the law, nor this without the Gospel. And they sat under the tree in sign of the Lord's passion, whereof they are the preachers.

« Behold she is in the tabernacle, » etc. ((STRAB.)) Abraham is without with the angels, Sara is in the tabernacle: because it belongs to the strong and the learned to preach openly, to instruct by examples: to the weak and the unwise, to learn and to be subject.

«

And she shall have a son, » etc. God promises a son to the barren Sara, saying: About this time I will come; he signifies not the time, but the quality of his coming, since through the son promised again the faithful people was to be born. Whence Isa. LIV and Gal. IV: « Rejoice, thou barren, that travailest not, » etc.

« Which when she had heard, etc. ((AUG. Quaest in Gen. )) Sara is reproved because she laughed, and not Abraham, although he had laughed in like manner; because Abraham's laughter was of wonder, Sara's of doubt, which he could discern who knows the heart. Sara denies that she laughed, whereas she cannot be hidden from God, but perhaps she thought that they were men. But Abraham understood God, yet in rendering the offices of humanity, which are necessary only to weak flesh; it is strange: unless he first judged them men, but men in whom he understood God to speak, certain signs of the divine majesty appearing: as Scripture often testifies that God appeared in men, but afterward they knew that they had been angels.

« And they were, » etc. The age of the elderly is less than that of the old, even though the old be called elderly. Whence, according to the physicians, an elderly man cannot get children of an elderly woman, even though the courses of women still flow. According to this Abraham wonders at the power of God concerning the promise of a son, and we can take it that the Apostle set down this miracle. For the body was not altogether dead for generation, if the woman had been of youthful age: but of one of advanced age he could not beget: for of Cethura he afterward begot, because she was young. For the physicians hand down that an old man cannot beget of a woman of more advanced age (even though the courses of women befall her), but of a young one he can. Again a woman of advanced age, even though the courses of women still befall her, cannot bear by an elderly man, but by a young one she can. It was therefore a miracle, because both were old and of advanced age, and the courses of women had ceased for Sara.
« Shall I give myself to pleasure? » etc. ((GREG. lib. IX Moral., c. 51.)) The care of the flesh, etc., *as far as* what else does our mind bring forth than joy?
« I did not laugh, etc. ((AMBR.)) Or she therefore denied that she had laughed, because she was ignorant; she therefore laughed, because she prophesied.

*I have loved.* ((ID.)) This the sheep says which had strayed, the son returned, the pilgrim of this world.

((CASS.)) *I have loved.* Not for the temporal goods given to me, as the unbelievers do, but *because,* etc. God is loved even by unbelievers because he gives good things; whence: *I will praise thee when thou shalt do well to him ((Psal. XLVIII))*. He is loved perfectly, him *eum*; read *cum*, "when" the mind is not moved by adverse things, but is kindled by hope: which manner he afterwards expounds, *I have loved.* Not because he made me a king, or gave me prosperity, but because he hears my prayer in straits.

*And in my days.* ((AUG.)) Namely of my misery, which days I made for myself by sinning, which are full of labour and sorrow, that is, of the old rottenness.

*I will call upon.* Which is not without faith; whence the Apostle: *How shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? ((Rom. X.))* When therefore he says, *they shall call upon,* note that the lover is not idle. In which, *They have compassed me,* etc. Or, in the days of salvation, that is, in the time of fulness; whence: *Behold, now is the acceptable time,* etc. ((II Cor. VI)).

notes.text: Being justified by faith — This is the sum of the preceding chapters. We have peace with God - Being enemies to God no longer, ver. 10; neither fearing his wrath, ver. 9. We have peace, hope, love, and power over sin, the sum of the fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth chapters. These are the fruits of justifying faith: where these are not, that faith is not.
Into this grace — This state of favour.

We glory in tribulations also — Which we are so far from esteeming a mark of God's displeasure, that we receive them as tokens of his fatherly love, whereby we are prepared for a more exalted happiness. The Jews objected to the persecuted state of the Christians as inconsistent with the people of the Messiah. It is therefore with great propriety that the apostle so often mentions the blessings arising from this very thing.
And patience works more experience of the sincerity of our grace, and of God's power and faithfulness.

Hope shameth us not — That is, gives us the highest glorying. We glory in this our hope, because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts - The divine conviction of God's love to us, and that love to God which is both the earnest and the beginning of heaven. By the Holy Ghost - The efficient cause of all these present blessings, and the earnest of those to come.

How can we now doubt of God's love? For when we were without strength — Either to think, will, or do anything good. In due time - Neither too soon nor too late; but in that very point of time which the wisdom of God knew to be more proper than any other. Christ died for the ungodly - Not only to set them a pattern, or to procure them power to follow it. It does not appear that this expression, of dying for any one, has any other signification than that of rescuing the life of another by laying down our own.

A just man — One who gives to all what is strictly their due The good man - One who is eminently holy; full of love, of compassion, kindness, mildness, of every heavenly and amiable temper. Perhaps-one-would-even-dare to die - Every word increases the strangeness of the thing, and declares even this to be something great and unusual.

But God recommendeth — A most elegant expression. Those are wont to be recommended to us, who were before either unknown to, or alienated from, us. While we were sinners - So far from being good, that we were not even just.

glossa.text: *From faith.* Above he said, justified freely by grace, lest faith itself be proud. Let not the faithful man say: that I may merit justification, I have faith: for it is answered him: what hast thou that thou hast not received? *Let us have peace,* we who have been reconciled to him through Christ, the minister of grace.
*Through whom.* He enumerates the benefits that are had from Christ.

*Tribulation.* That tribulation does not take away patience, charity brings about, which is the proper gift of the Holy Spirit.

*Hope.* That is, the certitude of future glory, which to human reason seems empty: but it is confirmed by the testimony of virtue, that is, of patience or of miracles.

*But hope.* Because it is in God, who does not deceive, not in lying man; and the pledge of this hope is the Spirit: for it is read: *Let the fountain of thy water be thine own, and let no stranger have communication with thee ((Eccli. V))*; he himself is the Spirit, whom the wicked cannot receive, and he is charity, which no one can have and be wicked. But a man can have the name of Christ and baptism, receive the body of the Lord, and have the other sacraments, and be wicked. Charity therefore is the proper gift of the Spirit, and the singular fountain.

*The charity of God.* Or: God loves us widely: and we have this in our hearts through the Spirit, who makes us understand the charity of God toward us.

*For why.* Since God loves us, or we love him through the Spirit, hope will be fulfilled: because unless it be so, Christ suffered in vain. And this is why Christ [suffered] for the ungodly, that is, for love of the ungodly, or in their stead: for the ungodly, not those who had been so of old and were not so then, but when we were weak in sins.

*According to the time,* that is, for three days only, lest thou despair of the power of him whose good will appears in his death: from whom we receive such earnests, in that he gave to the ungodly his own death, who keeps for the just his own life. He died for thee, O mortal man, that thou mayest live with him. He took upon himself our death, that he might give us his own life: he received from thee that whereby he might die for thee. He clothed himself with that wherein he might die for thee: he will clothe thee with that wherein thou mayest live with him. He clothed himself with mortal flesh in the virginity of his mother: he will clothe thee with everlasting life in the equality of the Father.

*Scarcely.* He says, *for a just man.* Perhaps for a good man: he shows both to be difficult and rare, but the one more difficult and more rare.

*For a just man,* etc. A man is just by reason of his exercise, who is also good; but there is also a good man who is not just, that is, one who was born in simplicity: an innocent who has not yet laboured to enlarge himself with goods, such as are the little ones cleansed in baptism; and although the just man is the better, yet the cause of innocence is the more pitiable, rather than that of justice, because justice of this kind is not without severity.

*While yet.* Behold, while he hated us according to our sins, he loved us according to that which is his own work: which also he did before the constitution of the world. It had to be said how much he loved us, lest we should despair; and what manner of men we were, lest we should be proud. There was another way also possible to God, who can do all things, but none more fitting for the healing of our misery. For what so lifts us up, and frees us from despair of immortality, as that he made so much of us, that a man should die for us?

notes.text: Because they were faint — In soul rather than in body. As sheep having no shepherd - And yet they had many teachers; they had scribes in every city. But they had none who cared for their souls, and none that were able, if they had been willing, to have wrought any deliverance. They had no pastors after God's own heart.

The harvest truly is great — When Christ came into the world, it was properly the time of harvest; till then it was the seed time only. But the labourers are few - Those whom God sends; who are holy, and convert sinners. Of others there are many. Luke x, 2.

The Lord of the harvest — Whose peculiar work and office it is, and who alone is able to do it: that he would thrust forth - for it is an employ not pleasing to flesh and blood; so full of reproach, labour, danger, temptation of every kind, that nature may well be averse to it. Those who never felt this, never yet knew what it is to be labourers in Christ's harvest. He sends them forth, when he calls them by his Spirit, furnishes them with grace and gifts for the work, and makes a way for them to be employed therein.

His twelve disciples — Hence it appears that he had already chosen out of his disciples, those whom he afterward termed apostles. The number seems to have relation to the twelve patriarchs, and the twelve tribes of Israel. Mark iii, 14; vi, 7; Luke vi, 13; ix, 1.
The first, Simon — The first who was called to a constant attendance on Christ; although Andrew had seen him before Simon. Acts i, 13.
Lebbeus — Commonly called Judas, the brother of James.
Iscariot — So called from Iscarioth, (the place of his birth, ) a town of the tribe of Ephraim, near the city of Samaria.

These twelve Jesus sent forth — Herein exercising his supreme authority, as God over all. None but God can give men authority to preach his word. Go not - Their commission was thus confined now, because the calling of the Gentiles was deferred till after the more plentiful effusion of the Holy Ghost on the day of pentecost. Enter not - Not to preach; but they might to buy what they wanted, John iv, 9.

Cast out devils — It is a great relief to the spirits of an infidel, sinking under a dread, that possibly the Gospel may be true, to find it observed by a learned brother, that the diseases therein ascribed to the operation of the devil have the very same symptoms with the natural diseases of lunacy, epilepsy, or convulsions; whence he readily and very willingly concludes, that the devil had no hand in them. But it were well to stop and consider a little. Suppose God should suffer an evil spirit to usurp the same power over a man's body, as the man himself has naturally; and suppose him actually to exercise that power; could we conclude the devil had no hand therein, because his body was bent in the very same manner wherein the man himself might have bent it naturally? And suppose God gives an evil spirit a greater power, to effect immediately the organ of the nerves in the brain, by irritating them to produce violent motions, or so relaxing them that they can produce little or no motion; still the symptoms will be those of over tense nerves, as in madness, epilepsies, convulsions; or of relaxed nerves, as in paralytic cases. But could we conclude thence that the devil had no hand in them? Will any man affirm that God cannot or will not, on any occasion whatever, give such a power to an evil spirit? Or that effects, the like of which may be produced by natural causes, cannot possibly be produced by preternatural? If this be possible, then he who affirms it was so, in any particular case, cannot be justly charged with falsehood, merely for affirming the reality of a possible thing. Yet in this manner are the evangelists treated by those unhappy men, who above all things dread the truth of the Gospel, because, if it is true, they are of all men the most miserable. Freely ye have received - All things; in particular the power of working miracles; freely give - Exert that power wherever you come. Mark vi, 7; Luke ix, 2.

glossa.text: *And having called together.* From the healing of Peter's mother-in-law, etc., *as far as* the centurion's servant healed. *Twelve.* These are the labourers who were to be sent, and who were to call the quarters of the four-square world to faith in the Trinity. That their preaching might have the weight of authority, power is given them to heal every infirmity.
*Peter and Andrew.* He joins the apostles in pairs and yokes, etc., *as far as* Christ, in whom he believed.
*Thomas.* The abyss: because by a sure faith he penetrated the depth of the divine power in the resurrection. Or, Thomas a twin, which in Greek is didymus, because of a doubting heart in believing.

*And Judas Scariothis.* A great example of teaching for us, since he who knew all things did not hesitate to choose a betrayer for a disciple and to ordain him an apostle. For Christ has a witness conscious of his own cleanness, since he does not hesitate to choose his own betrayer.

*Into the way.* After the resurrection he says: *Teach ye all nations.* But this beforehand: because the Jews must first be preached to, lest they have a cause for not receiving him, in that he sent the apostles to the Gentiles.

*The kingdom of heaven shall draw near.* Through faith the kingdom is near. For as one who sins is earth, so let the just man be heaven, in which God presides; whence it is said: *The kingdom of God is within you ((Luc. XVII))*, etc. Behold what they ought to preach: The kingdom of heaven shall draw near.

*Heal the sick.* The Church strengthens the sick by the standing of good work, raises the dead in sins, or without faith; cleanses the lepers sprinkled with errors, puts demons to flight by exorcisms. *Freely have you received.* Lest Judas, who had the purse, should wish to gather money out of the aforesaid power, the Lord suppresses his wickedness, saying: *Freely have you received,* etc. Here also he condemns the perfidy of the Simoniac heresy. Spiritual gifts are cheapened by a price.

notes.text: Thus shalt thou say to the house of Jacob, and the children of Israel — The people are called by the names both of Jacob and Israel, to mind them that they who had lately been as low as Jacob when he went to Padan-aram, were now grown as great as God made him when he came from thence, and was called Israel.

Ye have seen what I did unto the Egyptians, and how I bare you on Eagle's wings — An high expression of the wonderful tenderness God shewed for them. It notes great speed; God not only came upon the wing for their deliverance, but he hastened them out, as it were upon the wing. Also that he did it with great ease, with the strength as well as with the swiftness of an eagle. They that faint not, nor are weary, are said to mount up with wings as eagles, Isaiah xl, 31. Especially it notes God's particular care of them, and affection to them. Even Egypt was the nest in which these young ones were first formed as the embryo of a nation: when by the increase of their numbers they grew to some maturity, they were carried out of that nest. I brought you unto myself - They were brought not only into a state of liberty, but into covenant and communion with God. This, God aims at in all the gracious methods of his providence and grace, to bring us back to himself, from whom we have revolted, and to bring us home to himself, in whom alone we can be happy.

Then ye shall be a peculiar treasure to me — He doth not instance in any one particular favour, but expresseth it in that which was inclusive of all happiness, that he would be to them a God in covenant, and they should be to him a people. Nay you shall be a peculiar treasure: not that God was enriched by them, as a man is by his treasure, but he was pleased to value and esteem them as a man doth his treasure; they were precious in his sight. He took them under his special care and protection, as a treasure that is kept under lock and key. He distinguished them from, and dignified them above all people, as a people devoted to him, and to his service.

A kingdom of priests, a holy nation — All the Israelites, if compared with other people, were priests unto God, so near were they to him, so much employed in his immediate service, and such intimate communion they had with him. The tendency of the laws given them was to distinguish them from others, and engage them for God as a holy nation. Thus all believers are, through Christ, made to our God kings and priests, Rev. i, 6, a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, 1 Pet. ii, 9.

And Moses laid before their faces all these words — He not only explained to them what God had given him in charge, but put it to their choice, whether they would accept these promises upon these terms or no. His laying it to their faces speaks his laying it to their consciences.
And they answered together; all that the Lord hath spoken we will do — Thus accepting the Lord to be to them a God, and giving up themselves to be to him a people.

glossa.text:
*In the third month,* etc. ((ORIG.)) Another reading: *And the going out of the children of Israel from the land of Egypt was of the third month: on this day they came into the desert of Sina, and they set forward from Raphidim, and came into the desert of Sina, and Israel pitched there over against the mountain. And Moses went up into the mount of God, and the Lord called him from the mountain, saying: These things shalt thou say to the house of Jacob, and thou shalt announce to the children of Israel,* etc. And a little after: *Go down and charge the people, and thou shalt purify them today and tomorrow, and let them wash their garments, and let them be ready against the third day. For on the third day the Lord will come down upon mount Sina in the sight of all the people.* On this day the law is found to be given, which was written on tables of stone by the finger of God, as the things that follow teach. And this third day appears to be of the third month from the going out of the children of Israel from Egypt; from the day on which they kept the pasch, that is, immolated and ate the lamb, which was the fourteenth of the first month, as far as that on which the law is given, fifty days are numbered, seventeen namely of the first month, the rest from the fourteenth itself. Then all thirty of the second month, which make forty-seven, and the third of the third month, which from the solemnity of the slain lamb is the fiftieth; and by this, in that shadow of things to come, according to the feast day of the immolated lamb; because on the fiftieth day the law was given, written by the finger of God. So in the very truth of the New Testament, from the festival of the immolated Lamb Jesus Christ fifty days are numbered, wherein the Holy Spirit was given from the highest places, who is the finger of God.

*On this day,* etc. On the forty-seventh day, namely, after they went out of Egypt, on the first day, namely, of June, they came to mount Sina, and there, when the two days were passed in which they were sanctified, on the third, that is, the fiftieth, they received the law: and this is Pentecost.

((RAB.)) In Sina there was one station, but the greatest of all. For there the law was received, the tabernacle set up. There Exodus and the greatest part of Leviticus and all the books of the law were almost wholly written.

*But Moses,* etc. ((GREG., lib. VI Moral., cap. 27.)) Another reading: *But Moses went up into the mountain, and the Lord came down to him.* The mountain is the height of contemplation, into which we go up, that by gazing we may be lifted to those things which are beyond our weakness. But the Lord comes down, because, to saints who make much progress, he opens some small thing of himself.
*The wings of eagles.* He calls the teachings of the two Testaments, which bear us from the lowest things to the heavenly.
*You shall be to me a priestly kingdom,* etc. Members, namely, of the high priest who is to come into the kingdom of heaven.

*He set forth all the words,* etc. ((GREG.)) It is to be noted that the law is not thrust upon the unwary or the ignorant: but when the rewards which are due to those who keep it have been set forth, and the past benefits which they have already experienced, and the wonders, when of their own accord they devote themselves to the keeping of the law, the law is given to those who ask for it: so that according to their own promise, as men bound by a vow, those who violate it may be judged, and may not complain of violence done to them.

*A psalm in confession.* Confession is twofold; one is of praise, the other of sins. The confession of praise befits the perfect, the confession of sins those who are beginning *inicipientibus*; whence in this psalm the prophet admonishes to confession. ((CASS.)) This psalm teaches both to praise God unceasingly, and unceasingly to bewail our sins: because neither in evils is one to despair, nor in good things ought the mind to be lifted up. First he enjoins upon the perfect the chief kind of confession, that is, praise.

*Rejoice ye.* ((AUG.)) If the voice rejoices outwardly, etc., *as far as* and in what order and how wonderfully he made it. *All the earth.* Admonishing to praise. Not one corner of the earth does he exhort: but as he knows the blessing to have been sown everywhere, so from everywhere he requires jubilation. *Serve ye in gladness.* ((AUG.)) This servitude is not of bitterness, nor of indignation, but of happiness and of liberty. Let charity therefore make thee a servant, because truth has made thee free. Whence the Lord: *If you shall abide in my word, you shall be my disciples indeed: and you shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free ((Joan. VIII))*. 

*In gladness.* Because they are set free; not murmuring, as in the desert: whence he subjoins the reward.

*Enter ye into his sight.* It is a great thing to rejoice in the sight of so great a one. *Enter ye in.* ((CASS.)) Secondly, to those about to enter, the second kind of confession; nor let it be doubted, because mercy is with him.

notes.text: Being justified by faith — This is the sum of the preceding chapters. We have peace with God - Being enemies to God no longer, ver. 10; neither fearing his wrath, ver. 9. We have peace, hope, love, and power over sin, the sum of the fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth chapters. These are the fruits of justifying faith: where these are not, that faith is not.
Into this grace — This state of favour.

We glory in tribulations also — Which we are so far from esteeming a mark of God's displeasure, that we receive them as tokens of his fatherly love, whereby we are prepared for a more exalted happiness. The Jews objected to the persecuted state of the Christians as inconsistent with the people of the Messiah. It is therefore with great propriety that the apostle so often mentions the blessings arising from this very thing.
And patience works more experience of the sincerity of our grace, and of God's power and faithfulness.

Hope shameth us not — That is, gives us the highest glorying. We glory in this our hope, because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts - The divine conviction of God's love to us, and that love to God which is both the earnest and the beginning of heaven. By the Holy Ghost - The efficient cause of all these present blessings, and the earnest of those to come.

How can we now doubt of God's love? For when we were without strength — Either to think, will, or do anything good. In due time - Neither too soon nor too late; but in that very point of time which the wisdom of God knew to be more proper than any other. Christ died for the ungodly - Not only to set them a pattern, or to procure them power to follow it. It does not appear that this expression, of dying for any one, has any other signification than that of rescuing the life of another by laying down our own.

A just man — One who gives to all what is strictly their due The good man - One who is eminently holy; full of love, of compassion, kindness, mildness, of every heavenly and amiable temper. Perhaps-one-would-even-dare to die - Every word increases the strangeness of the thing, and declares even this to be something great and unusual.

But God recommendeth — A most elegant expression. Those are wont to be recommended to us, who were before either unknown to, or alienated from, us. While we were sinners - So far from being good, that we were not even just.

glossa.text: *From faith.* Above he said, justified freely by grace, lest faith itself be proud. Let not the faithful man say: that I may merit justification, I have faith: for it is answered him: what hast thou that thou hast not received? *Let us have peace,* we who have been reconciled to him through Christ, the minister of grace.
*Through whom.* He enumerates the benefits that are had from Christ.

*Tribulation.* That tribulation does not take away patience, charity brings about, which is the proper gift of the Holy Spirit.

*Hope.* That is, the certitude of future glory, which to human reason seems empty: but it is confirmed by the testimony of virtue, that is, of patience or of miracles.

*But hope.* Because it is in God, who does not deceive, not in lying man; and the pledge of this hope is the Spirit: for it is read: *Let the fountain of thy water be thine own, and let no stranger have communication with thee ((Eccli. V))*; he himself is the Spirit, whom the wicked cannot receive, and he is charity, which no one can have and be wicked. But a man can have the name of Christ and baptism, receive the body of the Lord, and have the other sacraments, and be wicked. Charity therefore is the proper gift of the Spirit, and the singular fountain.

*The charity of God.* Or: God loves us widely: and we have this in our hearts through the Spirit, who makes us understand the charity of God toward us.

*For why.* Since God loves us, or we love him through the Spirit, hope will be fulfilled: because unless it be so, Christ suffered in vain. And this is why Christ [suffered] for the ungodly, that is, for love of the ungodly, or in their stead: for the ungodly, not those who had been so of old and were not so then, but when we were weak in sins.

*According to the time,* that is, for three days only, lest thou despair of the power of him whose good will appears in his death: from whom we receive such earnests, in that he gave to the ungodly his own death, who keeps for the just his own life. He died for thee, O mortal man, that thou mayest live with him. He took upon himself our death, that he might give us his own life: he received from thee that whereby he might die for thee. He clothed himself with that wherein he might die for thee: he will clothe thee with that wherein thou mayest live with him. He clothed himself with mortal flesh in the virginity of his mother: he will clothe thee with everlasting life in the equality of the Father.

*Scarcely.* He says, *for a just man.* Perhaps for a good man: he shows both to be difficult and rare, but the one more difficult and more rare.

*For a just man,* etc. A man is just by reason of his exercise, who is also good; but there is also a good man who is not just, that is, one who was born in simplicity: an innocent who has not yet laboured to enlarge himself with goods, such as are the little ones cleansed in baptism; and although the just man is the better, yet the cause of innocence is the more pitiable, rather than that of justice, because justice of this kind is not without severity.

*While yet.* Behold, while he hated us according to our sins, he loved us according to that which is his own work: which also he did before the constitution of the world. It had to be said how much he loved us, lest we should despair; and what manner of men we were, lest we should be proud. There was another way also possible to God, who can do all things, but none more fitting for the healing of our misery. For what so lifts us up, and frees us from despair of immortality, as that he made so much of us, that a man should die for us?

notes.text: Because they were faint — In soul rather than in body. As sheep having no shepherd - And yet they had many teachers; they had scribes in every city. But they had none who cared for their souls, and none that were able, if they had been willing, to have wrought any deliverance. They had no pastors after God's own heart.

The harvest truly is great — When Christ came into the world, it was properly the time of harvest; till then it was the seed time only. But the labourers are few - Those whom God sends; who are holy, and convert sinners. Of others there are many. Luke x, 2.

The Lord of the harvest — Whose peculiar work and office it is, and who alone is able to do it: that he would thrust forth - for it is an employ not pleasing to flesh and blood; so full of reproach, labour, danger, temptation of every kind, that nature may well be averse to it. Those who never felt this, never yet knew what it is to be labourers in Christ's harvest. He sends them forth, when he calls them by his Spirit, furnishes them with grace and gifts for the work, and makes a way for them to be employed therein.

His twelve disciples — Hence it appears that he had already chosen out of his disciples, those whom he afterward termed apostles. The number seems to have relation to the twelve patriarchs, and the twelve tribes of Israel. Mark iii, 14; vi, 7; Luke vi, 13; ix, 1.
The first, Simon — The first who was called to a constant attendance on Christ; although Andrew had seen him before Simon. Acts i, 13.
Lebbeus — Commonly called Judas, the brother of James.
Iscariot — So called from Iscarioth, (the place of his birth, ) a town of the tribe of Ephraim, near the city of Samaria.

These twelve Jesus sent forth — Herein exercising his supreme authority, as God over all. None but God can give men authority to preach his word. Go not - Their commission was thus confined now, because the calling of the Gentiles was deferred till after the more plentiful effusion of the Holy Ghost on the day of pentecost. Enter not - Not to preach; but they might to buy what they wanted, John iv, 9.

Cast out devils — It is a great relief to the spirits of an infidel, sinking under a dread, that possibly the Gospel may be true, to find it observed by a learned brother, that the diseases therein ascribed to the operation of the devil have the very same symptoms with the natural diseases of lunacy, epilepsy, or convulsions; whence he readily and very willingly concludes, that the devil had no hand in them. But it were well to stop and consider a little. Suppose God should suffer an evil spirit to usurp the same power over a man's body, as the man himself has naturally; and suppose him actually to exercise that power; could we conclude the devil had no hand therein, because his body was bent in the very same manner wherein the man himself might have bent it naturally? And suppose God gives an evil spirit a greater power, to effect immediately the organ of the nerves in the brain, by irritating them to produce violent motions, or so relaxing them that they can produce little or no motion; still the symptoms will be those of over tense nerves, as in madness, epilepsies, convulsions; or of relaxed nerves, as in paralytic cases. But could we conclude thence that the devil had no hand in them? Will any man affirm that God cannot or will not, on any occasion whatever, give such a power to an evil spirit? Or that effects, the like of which may be produced by natural causes, cannot possibly be produced by preternatural? If this be possible, then he who affirms it was so, in any particular case, cannot be justly charged with falsehood, merely for affirming the reality of a possible thing. Yet in this manner are the evangelists treated by those unhappy men, who above all things dread the truth of the Gospel, because, if it is true, they are of all men the most miserable. Freely ye have received - All things; in particular the power of working miracles; freely give - Exert that power wherever you come. Mark vi, 7; Luke ix, 2.

glossa.text: *And having called together.* From the healing of Peter's mother-in-law, etc., *as far as* the centurion's servant healed. *Twelve.* These are the labourers who were to be sent, and who were to call the quarters of the four-square world to faith in the Trinity. That their preaching might have the weight of authority, power is given them to heal every infirmity.
*Peter and Andrew.* He joins the apostles in pairs and yokes, etc., *as far as* Christ, in whom he believed.
*Thomas.* The abyss: because by a sure faith he penetrated the depth of the divine power in the resurrection. Or, Thomas a twin, which in Greek is didymus, because of a doubting heart in believing.

*And Judas Scariothis.* A great example of teaching for us, since he who knew all things did not hesitate to choose a betrayer for a disciple and to ordain him an apostle. For Christ has a witness conscious of his own cleanness, since he does not hesitate to choose his own betrayer.

*Into the way.* After the resurrection he says: *Teach ye all nations.* But this beforehand: because the Jews must first be preached to, lest they have a cause for not receiving him, in that he sent the apostles to the Gentiles.

*The kingdom of heaven shall draw near.* Through faith the kingdom is near. For as one who sins is earth, so let the just man be heaven, in which God presides; whence it is said: *The kingdom of God is within you ((Luc. XVII))*, etc. Behold what they ought to preach: The kingdom of heaven shall draw near.

*Heal the sick.* The Church strengthens the sick by the standing of good work, raises the dead in sins, or without faith; cleanses the lepers sprinkled with errors, puts demons to flight by exorcisms. *Freely have you received.* Lest Judas, who had the purse, should wish to gather money out of the aforesaid power, the Lord suppresses his wickedness, saying: *Freely have you received,* etc. Here also he condemns the perfidy of the Simoniac heresy. Spiritual gifts are cheapened by a price.

registers.label: Spare
lines: Three strangers came to Abraham's tent, and he ran to meet them.
God comes to us, and we will not turn away.
Sarah laughed at a promise too good to be true.
Is anything too wonderful for the Lord?
The harvest is plentiful, the laborers few.
Send us out; we are willing to go.
Come, let us worship the God who keeps his word.
We come, and we are sent. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Stand with Abraham in the heat of the day and look up — the fields stretch out, heavy and golden, ready.
Lord of the harvest, send us out.
At the tent he set bread and meat before strangers, and the strangers carried a promise that made Sarah laugh.
Lord of the harvest, send us out.
Jesus looks over the crowds, harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd, and his heart breaks for them.
Lord of the harvest, send us out.
So he calls us by name and hands us the work: heal, proclaim, give freely what you have freely received.
Lord of the harvest, send us out. Here we are; send us!

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: Abraham ran to welcome the strangers at his tent.
Lord of the harvest, send us out.
They carried a promise that set Sarah laughing.
Lord of the harvest, send us out.
Jesus sees the crowds like sheep without a shepherd.
Lord of the harvest, send us out.
Come, let us worship, then go where we are sent.
Lord of the harvest, send us out. Amen.
